questions.q: Which GPU memory tier is the fastest but also the smallest per thread?
options: Global memory (HBM)
L2 cache
Shared memory
Registers
questions.explain: Registers are per-thread, the fastest possible storage, but limited to only a few hundred values per thread.

questions.q: What makes shared memory different from L2 cache?
options: Shared memory is slower than L2 cache
Shared memory is explicitly managed by the programmer with __shared__, while L2 cache is managed automatically
Shared memory is shared across the entire GPU, while L2 cache is per-block
Shared memory does not exist on modern GPUs
questions.explain: Shared memory is on-chip, per-block memory that the programmer explicitly allocates and manages with __shared__. L2 cache is GPU-wide and managed automatically by the hardware.

questions.q: What does it mean for a kernel to be "memory-bound"?
options: The kernel uses too many registers to compile
The kernel's runtime is limited by how fast data can be moved, not by compute capacity
The kernel only works on CPUs
The kernel has a memory leak
questions.explain: A memory-bound kernel spends more time waiting for data to arrive from memory than it does computing, because GPU compute throughput usually exceeds memory bandwidth.

questions.q: In the sumBlock example kernel, why does it copy data into a __shared__ array before processing?
options: To avoid using any global memory at all
So every thread in the block can reuse the cached copy instead of repeatedly reading from slower global memory
Because __shared__ arrays are required for all CUDA kernels
To increase the number of registers available
questions.explain: Reading from global memory once into shared memory lets all threads in the block reuse that fast, on-chip copy rather than each one re-reading from the much slower global memory tier.

questions.q: Where does a PyTorch tensor live by default once moved with .to('cuda')?
options: Only in CPU RAM
In the GPU's L2 cache
In the GPU's global memory (HBM)
In CUDA registers
questions.explain: A PyTorch tensor moved to a GPU is allocated in global memory (HBM), the large memory pool most code and tools mean by "GPU memory".
